title: APIs and Data Exchange
eyebrow: System boundaries · How software asks other software for work or data
summary: Follow one application asking an invoice service for work, then expand that simple conversation into the real rules an API needs: operations, inputs, responses, errors, security, retries, pagination, webhooks, GraphQL, events, and safe change over time.
prerequisites: How the Web Works is helpful for HTTP and request/response terminology. This guide briefly re-establishes the parts it relies on.
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript is helpful for the browser Fetch example, but the API concepts do not depend on frontend expertise.
learningOutcomes: Explain an API as an agreed software boundary containing operations, inputs, outcomes, errors, and change rules rather than as 'just a URL'.
Design and evaluate predictable HTTP requests, JSON shapes, errors, authentication/authorization, pagination, caching, timeouts, retries, and idempotent writes.
Choose among ordinary request-response APIs, GraphQL, webhooks, event streams, and local library APIs from the timing and coupling the interaction actually needs.

heroVisual.title: An API begins as one program asking another program for something
heroVisual.caption: The difficult production details grow from a simple need: both sides must agree on how to ask, what information is required, and what each possible outcome means.

nodes.label: Consumer
nodes.detail: The software that wants data or an action.

nodes.label: Operation + input
nodes.detail: The consumer states what it wants and provides the required information.

nodes.label: Provider boundary
nodes.detail: The receiving software authenticates, validates, authorizes, and routes the request.

nodes.label: Application work
nodes.detail: Business logic reads or changes authoritative data and calls other services when needed.

nodes.label: Outcome
nodes.detail: The provider returns data, an error, or later sends an event according to the agreed rules.

sections.title: 1. Start with a software conversation, not the word API
sections.summary: If one program needs another program to create an invoice, both sides need an agreed way to express the request and interpret the result.

blocks.text: Suppose a checkout application needs an invoice service to create an invoice. The checkout side must be able to say 'create an invoice for this customer in USD.' The invoice side must know which operation is being requested, what fields are required, what values are valid, what success returns, and what failure looks like. That agreed interface is an API, an Application Programming Interface. An API can exist inside one process or across a network; a web API commonly uses HTTP to carry the messages.

items.title: Provider
items.summary: The software exposing the capability or data.

items.title: Operation
items.summary: The capability the consumer is asking for.

items.title: Input
items.summary: Information the provider needs to attempt that operation.

items.title: Outcome
items.summary: What success, rejection, missing data, or internal failure means and what information is returned.

blocks.title: API contract
blocks.body: The API contract is the testable agreement at the boundary: available operations, accepted inputs, returned data, errors, side effects, security expectations, timing/operational behavior, and rules for changing the interface. Documentation describes the contract; validation and tests help enforce it.

blocks.prompt: If two services both use HTTP but disagree about required fields and what a 200 response contains, do they have a dependable API contract?
blocks.explanation: HTTP gives the messages transport-level and application-level semantics such as methods and status codes, but the software still needs agreement about its own operations and data. A URL plus JSON is not enough to make an interface predictable.

sections.title: 2. HTTP gives a web API standard request and response semantics
sections.summary: Use HTTP's existing meanings where they fit instead of making every action look like the same generic message.

blocks.text: For an HTTP API, a method describes the request semantics, the request target identifies a resource or endpoint, headers carry metadata, and an optional body carries content. The response uses a status code, headers, and often a body. Respecting those meanings gives clients, caches, proxies, monitoring tools, and developers more predictable behavior.

rows: 200 if found or 404 if that resource is not found.
201 when a new resource is created, commonly with information identifying it.
200/204 when replaced, or 201 when the contract permits creation there.
A success result or a structured validation/conflict response.
204 or another explicitly documented domain result.
blocks.caption: Common resource-oriented HTTP operations

blocks.explanation: POST asks the invoices collection to process a creation request. Content-Type says the body is JSON. The body contains the operation input. Idempotency-Key is an application-specific request field in APIs that define this pattern so a safe retry can be recognized as the same intended creation instead of creating another invoice.

blocks.title: REST is not a synonym for JSON over HTTP
blocks.body: REST is an architectural style with constraints broader than choosing HTTP methods and JSON. In day-to-day API design, the practical baseline is to make the interface coherent and use HTTP semantics, representations, caching behavior, links where they are useful, and stateless request handling deliberately rather than attaching the REST label to any endpoint.

sections.title: 3. Both sides need the same understanding of the data shape
sections.summary: Field names alone are not a complete data agreement. Types, required values, units, nullability, time rules, allowed states, and validation behavior are part of the contract.

visual.title: A useful schema describes more than JSON syntax
visual.caption: A schema is a defined description of data shape and constraints. Machine-readable formats can help tools generate validation, documentation, or clients, but meaning still has to be designed correctly.

nodes.label: Types and presence
nodes.detail: String, number, object, required, optional, nullable, or omitted.

nodes.label: Meaning
nodes.detail: Units, identifiers, time zones, precision, enumerated states, and domain rules.

nodes.label: Validation
nodes.detail: What the provider accepts, rejects, normalizes, or defaults.

blocks.explanation: id is the resource identifier. status is constrained by the invoice state model. amount carries currency beside an integer number of minor units so the unit and rounding model are explicit. createdAt uses an ISO/RFC-compatible timestamp with Z to state UTC rather than leaving the time zone implied.

blocks.text: A schema is a formal or documented description of a data shape and its constraints. OpenAPI can describe HTTP APIs and their schemas; GraphQL defines a typed schema as part of its query system; JSON Schema is another family of schema vocabularies. A schema is valuable because consumers, validators, tests, and documentation can share a more precise definition than prose alone. It does not remove the need to explain business meaning.

items: Distinguish required, optional, nullable, and omitted values.
State units, precision, encoding, identifier formats, and time-zone rules.
Define allowed enum/state values and how unknown values are handled.
Document defaults and whether the server stores or merely derives them.
Do not expose secrets or internal implementation details merely because a field exists inside the service.

sections.title: 4. Errors need machine-readable structure and useful human meaning
sections.summary: A status code can categorize an outcome, but clients often need stable details to decide what to show or do next.

blocks.text: A good error response separates a stable machine-readable category from a human-readable explanation and from request-specific details. RFC 9457 defines Problem Details for HTTP APIs, a standard format for carrying structured problem information without inventing a completely new error envelope for every API. It replaced the older RFC 7807.

blocks.code:
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/unsupported-currency",
  "title": "Currency is not supported",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Use one of USD, EUR, or CAD.",
  "instance": "/requests/req_9"
}
blocks.explanation: type identifies the kind of problem, title gives a short human description, status repeats the HTTP status when represented here, detail explains this occurrence, and instance can identify the particular occurrence. An API can define extensions when the problem type needs additional structured fields.

items.title: 400 Bad Request
items.summary: The request is malformed or otherwise cannot be processed as a valid request according to the API's rules.

items.title: 401 Unauthorized
items.summary: HTTP uses this status when authentication credentials are missing or not accepted for the protected request.

items.title: 403 Forbidden
items.summary: The server understood the request but refuses to authorize it under the applicable policy.
items.example: Authenticated user cannot approve this invoice

items.title: 404 Not Found
items.summary: The target resource is not found, or the server chooses not to reveal its existence under the contract.

items.title: 409 Conflict
items.summary: The request conflicts with the current resource state in a way the client may be able to resolve.
items.example: Attempt to edit an already-finalized invoice

items.title: 5xx
items.summary: The server failed to fulfill a request that reached it; clients should not assume every 5xx is safe to retry blindly.

sections.title: 5. Proving identity and granting permission are different decisions
sections.summary: Authentication establishes who or what is calling. Authorization decides whether that caller may perform this operation on this resource.

rows: Can the client communicate with this server over a protected channel?
Who or what is making this request?
Validate a session, signed token, or service credential.
May this established identity perform this action on this resource?
User may view invoice 42 but may not refund it.
Is the supplied input structurally and semantically acceptable?
Currency must be supported and amount must be within domain limits.
How much request activity is allowed within the policy window?
Which security-relevant action occurred, under which identity, and when?
Record invoice approval with actor and request correlation id.
blocks.caption: Security controls complement one another rather than replacing one another

blocks.title: Do not ship privileged credentials to browser code
blocks.body: Anything delivered to a browser is under the control of the person using that browser and can be inspected. Public client identifiers may be designed for exposure, but server secrets and credentials granting privileged authority belong in a trusted server-side environment.

blocks.prompt: A request includes a valid login token proving Alice's identity. Does that alone prove Alice may delete invoice 42?
blocks.explanation: Authentication established who the caller is. Authorization must separately evaluate whether that identity has permission for this operation on this particular resource and under the current policy/state.

sections.title: 6. Real APIs must behave predictably when data is large or networks fail
sections.summary: Pagination, caching, deadlines, retries, and idempotency are not optional polish once an API operates across unreliable networks and changing workloads.

visual.title: Different reliability tools solve different problems
visual.caption: Using one of these mechanisms does not automatically provide the others.

nodes.label: Pagination
nodes.detail: Bounds how much collection data is returned at once.

nodes.label: Caching
nodes.detail: Reuses a representation while the contract says reuse remains valid.

nodes.label: Timeout/deadline
nodes.detail: Bounds how long the caller is willing to wait for remote work.

nodes.label: Retry
nodes.detail: Repeats an eligible failed operation under controlled conditions.

nodes.label: Idempotency
nodes.detail: Defines how repeating an equivalent operation avoids unintended additional effects.

items.title: Cursor pagination
items.summary: The server returns a bounded page and an opaque cursor representing where a later request should continue in the ordered result set.
items.whenToUse: Useful when stable traversal through a changing ordered collection matters more than jumping directly to arbitrary page numbers.

items.title: Caching and validators
items.summary: Clients or intermediaries can reuse responses according to HTTP caching rules; validators such as ETag can let a client ask whether a representation changed.

items.title: Timeout or deadline
items.summary: The caller stops waiting after a known bound instead of allowing a remote dependency to hang forever.
items.example: Abort a fetch after the operation deadline

items.title: Backoff and jitter
items.summary: Backoff increases delay between retries; jitter adds variation so many clients do not retry in lockstep.
items.whenToUse: For eligible transient failures when retrying is safe and bounded.
items.avoidWhen: Do not turn permanent validation errors into repeated load.

items.title: Idempotency
items.summary: A contract property that lets equivalent repeated requests have the defined same intended effect rather than duplicating side effects.
items.whenToUse: Important when a write may need to be retried after the client cannot tell whether the first attempt completed.

blocks.text: A network timeout creates uncertainty: the caller knows it stopped waiting, but it may not know whether the provider did nothing, completed the operation just before the connection was lost, or is still working. Retrying a read is often simpler than retrying a side-effecting write. For writes, the API's operation semantics and idempotency design determine whether repeating the request can safely avoid duplicate effects.

blocks.title: Retries can amplify an outage
blocks.body: If thousands of callers retry immediately and repeatedly when a dependency is already unhealthy, retry traffic adds load at the worst time. Use eligibility rules, exponential or otherwise appropriate backoff, jitter, attempt limits, a total deadline, and observability.

blocks.prompt: A client times out after POST /invoices. It does not know whether the server created the invoice. Why can immediately repeating the same write be dangerous?
blocks.answer: The first request may already have succeeded, so an unprotected retry can create a second unintended invoice.
blocks.explanation: Timeout describes what the caller observed, not necessarily what the provider did. A well-designed idempotency contract can let the provider recognize the retried logical operation and return the established result instead of repeating the side effect.

sections.title: 7. Choose the communication style from who needs to talk, when, and how
sections.summary: There is no single API style that is automatically more advanced. The right mechanism follows the interaction's timing, query flexibility, delivery guarantees, and ownership boundaries.

rows: A caller asks for a bounded operation and expects a direct response.
Resource/operation semantics, schemas, errors, caching, retries, and compatibility.
Consumers benefit from selecting fields through a typed query schema and composing related data requests.
Schema design, resolver behavior, authorization, query cost limits, caching strategy, and evolution.
A provider needs to notify a registered consumer by sending that consumer an HTTP request after an event.
Authentication/signatures, delivery retries, duplicate handling, replay resistance, ordering assumptions, and endpoint availability.
Producers and consumers should be decoupled in time and multiple consumers may react independently.
Event schemas/evolution, delivery semantics, duplication, ordering, partitioning, lag, dead-letter/recovery strategy, and observability.
Both sides run in the same process and direct language-level calls are appropriate.
Package/version compatibility and in-process failure boundaries rather than network delivery.
blocks.caption: Pick the smallest interaction model that actually satisfies the requirement

blocks.title: Webhook
blocks.body: A webhook is an HTTP callback pattern: a provider sends an HTTP request to a consumer-provided endpoint when a defined event occurs. Because delivery crosses the network, the consumer must be prepared for retries, duplicates, delayed delivery, authentication/signature verification, and provider-specific ordering guarantees.

blocks.title: Do not add an event platform just to avoid a normal function or HTTP call
blocks.body: Asynchronous messaging can reduce time coupling and support many independent consumers, but it also introduces delivery state, duplicate handling, schema evolution, observability, and operational infrastructure. Use it when those trade-offs solve a real interaction need.

sections.title: 8. An API is not dependable if changing it silently breaks its consumers
sections.summary: Compatibility is part of the contract. A new deployment can keep the same URL and JSON syntax while still breaking callers through changed meaning or behavior.

items.title: Classify the proposed change
items.explanation: Adding an optional field may be compatible for tolerant consumers; removing or renaming a required field, changing meaning, narrowing accepted values, changing nullability, or altering timing/side effects can break callers.
items.result: Compatibility risk is explicit before release.

items.title: Publish a precise definition
items.explanation: Maintain documentation and, where practical, machine-readable schemas such as OpenAPI or GraphQL schema definitions that describe the supported interface.
items.result: Humans and automated checks can compare against the same contract.

items.title: Test representative consumers
items.explanation: Contract tests verify assumptions at the boundary; examples and real client tests expose behavior that schema shape alone may not capture.
items.result: Unexpected incompatibility is more likely to appear before production.

items.title: Deprecate visibly
items.explanation: Deprecation means an interface is still available but planned for replacement/removal. Publish the replacement, migration steps, timing, and support window.
items.result: Consumers have a concrete migration path.

items.title: Observe actual use before removal
items.explanation: Measure versions, endpoints, fields, errors, and deprecated operations so removal is based on evidence rather than assumptions.
items.result: The provider can distinguish 'documented as old' from 'actually unused.'

items: Treat changed field meaning as a possible breaking change even when the JSON shape is identical.
Adding enum values can break consumers that assumed the old set was exhaustive.
Changing from omitted to null, or vice versa, can break strict clients.
Version numbers or URL prefixes do not replace a migration and deprecation strategy.
Observe latency, error rate, saturation, retry behavior, and consumer adoption during migrations.

glossary.definition: An Application Programming Interface: a defined boundary through which software can request capabilities or data from another component.
The testable agreement describing operations, inputs, outcomes, errors, security/operational behavior, and change rules at a software boundary.
A formal or documented definition of a data shape and its constraints.
The process of establishing who or what a caller is.
The decision about whether an established caller may perform a particular action on a particular resource under current policy.
Pagination that continues from an opaque position in an ordered result set instead of relying only on numbered pages.
A retry strategy that waits between attempts, commonly increasing the delay for later attempts.
Random or varied delay added to retry timing so many clients are less likely to retry simultaneously.
A defined property where repeating an equivalent operation does not create additional unintended effects beyond the contract's intended result.
An HTTP callback sent by a provider to a registered consumer endpoint when a defined event occurs.
A notice that an interface is still available but is planned to be replaced or removed, accompanied by a migration path and timeline.
